problem_statement:
MetaCopyDetectionMiddleware warns on requests created by get_retry_request()
`get_retry_request()` is meant to be called from spider callbacks, but `MetaCopyDetectionMiddleware` warns that the spider “copied” response.meta: ['cache_timestamp', 'download_latency', 'retry_times'].
hints_text:
Reproduced on master. `get_retry_request(response.request, ...)` returns `request.copy()`, and `response.request.meta` *is* `response.meta`. So the retry carries `download_latency`, `cache_timestamp` and its new `retry_times`, which is exactly what the middleware looks for, even though carrying them is the whole point of a retry.

I fixed it in the middleware instead of in `get_retry_request`: skip the check when the yielded request looks like a retry of the response's own request, meaning same url/method/body and `retry_times` one higher than the source. A plain `meta=response.meta` copy keeps the same `retry_times`, so that still warns, and so does `retry_times` set on some unrelated request.

```diff
diff --git a/scrapy/spidermiddlewares/metacopy.py b/scrapy/spidermiddlewares/metacopy.py
index a46e820..a7e8fdf 100644
--- a/scrapy/spidermiddlewares/metacopy.py
+++ b/scrapy/spidermiddlewares/metacopy.py
@@ -47,7 +47,7 @@ class MetaCopyDetectionMiddleware(BaseSpiderMiddleware):
         if response is None:
             return request
 
-        if not self._warned:
+        if not self._warned and not self._is_retry(request, response):
             found = self._keys & request.meta.keys()
             if found:
                 spider_name = type(self.crawler.spider).__name__
@@ -63,3 +63,22 @@ class MetaCopyDetectionMiddleware(BaseSpiderMiddleware):
                 self._warned = True
 
         return request
+
+    @staticmethod
+    def _is_retry(request: Request, response: Response) -> bool:
+        """Return ``True`` if *request* looks like a retry of the request of
+        *response*, e.g. one built with
+        :func:`~scrapy.downloadermiddlewares.retry.get_retry_request`.
+
+        A retry is a copy of the source request, so it carries its meta keys
+        on purpose.
+        """
+        source = response.request
+        if source is None:
+            return False
+        return (
+            request.meta.get("retry_times") == source.meta.get("retry_times", 0) + 1
+            and request.url == source.url
+            and request.method == source.method
+            and request.body == source.body
+        )
```

Tests added to `tests/test_spidermiddleware_metacopy.py`:
- `get_retry_request()` on a response with `download_latency`/`cache_timestamp`: no warning, request passes through
- a second retry (`retry_times` 1 → 2): no warning
- same-URL request with copied meta (same `retry_times`): still warns
- `retry_times` on a different request (POST): still warns

The first two fail on master and pass with the patch. `tests/test_spidermiddleware*.py` (175) and `test_downloadermiddleware_retry.py` pass, and ruff check/format are clean.

Another way to do it would be a private marker that `get_retry_request` sets, but that ends up in user-visible meta, so I went with the heuristic. Happy to open a PR either way.

+                raise ValueError(f"{MyComponent.__qualname__} requires asyncio support.")

+code that calls asyncio APIs, awaits on futures and uses

+automatically choose a Twisted-based implementation when asyncio is not
+available:

+.. autofunction:: scrapy.utils.asyncio.call_later
+.. autofunction:: scrapy.utils.asyncio.create_looping_call

problem_statement:
Removing the non-asyncio reactor support
I think it's time to at least open this discussion.

**Pros**: removes a lot of compatibility code and poorly tested alternative code paths from Scrapy, simplifies the docs. Allows us to deprecate `TelnetConsole` in favor of `aioconsole` and/or `ipykernel`.
**Cons**: losing possible performance benefits? Some Windows/asyncio/3.14+ incompatibilities? Losing some platform-specific reactors that are based on different polling mechanisms than `AsyncioSelectorReactor`?

> Losing some platform-specific reactors that are based on different polling mechanisms than AsyncioSelectorReactor?

As for this, it seems that both Twisted (see [this](https://docs.twisted.org/en/stable/core/howto/choosing-reactor.html) and [this](https://github.com/twisted/twisted/blob/9e9922df02ab8a57d4efb3af6756c7bc3353cd8c/src/twisted/internet/default.py#L28)) and asyncio (see [this](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-eventloop.html#event-loop-implementations) and [this](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/c8ea8676d931a3b42a428123070628f9ba8390db/Lib/selectors.py#L592)) already use the best available polling API by default, with the exception of Windows IOCP (which is not used by default in Twisted because it's not ready and explicitly switched off by Scrapy in asyncio when using a reactor because Twisted can't use it), and in a vacuum I find it unlikely that someone would want e.g. `select` over `poll`.
Sounds good to me. And if we give it the regular deprecation treatment, that will give users a while to argue against the removal if they have a good reason.

problem_statement:
RobotsTxtMiddleware shares rules between HTTP and HTTPS with the same authority
### Description

`RobotsTxtMiddleware` caches the parsed robots rules by `netloc` only. Requests to `http://host:port` and `https://host:port` consequently share one parser, even though their robots files belong to different scheme/authority combinations. If the HTTP version allows a URL but the HTTPS version disallows it, the HTTPS URL may be fetched after the HTTP robots file was cached.

[RFC 9309 section 2.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309#section-2.3) identifies the robots file using the URI's scheme and authority. This is about respecting crawler directives, not treating `robots.txt` as access control.

### Steps to Reproduce

Save the following as `repro.py` and run each command in a fresh process:

```sh
python repro.py httpsonly
python repro.py mixed
```

The local server supports HTTP and HTTPS on the same port so the two URLs have exactly the same `netloc`. A temporary self-signed certificate is generated using the `openssl` CLI. All traffic stays on localhost.

```python
import os
import socket
import ssl
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import threading
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer

problem_statement:
SitemapSpider includes trailing robots.txt comment in sitemap request URL
### Description

`SitemapSpider` includes trailing `robots.txt` comments in the extracted sitemap URL. For a line like `Sitemap: http://host/sitemap.xml # generated sitemap`, the space before `#` is encoded as `%20` in the request path. The server receives `/sitemap.xml%20` and can return 404, so the spider never discovers the pages in the sitemap.

[Robots Exclusion Protocol syntax](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309#section-2.2) allows trailing comments in `robots.txt` lines; sitemap records are a commonly supported extension. The issue occurs in `sitemap_urls_from_robots`: the value is stripped but the comment is not removed.

### Steps to Reproduce

Save this script as `repro.py` and run `python repro.py plain`, then `python repro.py comment`. It starts a local HTTP server and runs an actual `SitemapSpider` against it; no external site is contacted.

```python
import os
import sys
import threading
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer

from scrapy.crawler import CrawlerProcess
from scrapy.spiders import SitemapSpider

seen = []
comment = ' # generated sitemap' if sys.argv[1] == 'comment' else ''

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        seen.append(self.path)
        base = f'http://127.0.0.1:{self.server.server_port}'
        if self.path == '/robots.txt':
            data = f'Sitemap: {base}/sitemap.xml{comment}\n'.encode()
            content_type = 'text/plain'
        elif self.path == '/sitemap.xml':
            data = (
                '<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">'
                f'<url><loc>{base}/page</loc></url></urlset>'
            ).encode()
            content_type = 'application/xml'
        elif self.path == '/page':
            data, content_type = b'ok', 'text/plain'
        else:
            self.send_error(404)
            return
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header('Content-Type', content_type)
        self.send_header('Content-Length', str(len(data)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(data)

    def log_message(self, *args):
        pass

server = ThreadingHTTPServer(('127.0.0.1', 0), Handler)
threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
os.environ['no_proxy'] = '127.0.0.1'

class Demo(SitemapSpider):
    name = 'demo'
    sitemap_urls = [f'http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_port}/robots.txt']

    def parse(self, response):
        yield {'url': response.url}

process = CrawlerProcess(settings={'LOG_ENABLED': False, 'ROBOTSTXT_OBEY': False})
process.crawl(Demo)
process.start()
server.shutdown()
server.server_close()
print(sys.argv[1], seen)
```

Actual:

```text
$ python repro.py plain
plain ['/robots.txt', '/sitemap.xml', '/page']
$ python repro.py comment
comment ['/robots.txt', '/sitemap.xml%20']
```

**Expected behavior:** The trailing comment should not change the URL; both runs should request `/sitemap.xml` and `/page`. Encoded URL data such as `%23` should remain intact.

**Reproduces how often:** Every run in this local test.

problem_statement:
Request.from_curl() doesn't decode escapes in $'...' strings, and fails on \'
### Description

#5901 (fixing #5899) made `$'...'` strings parse by turning `$'` into a plain `'`. The backslash escapes inside them are never decoded, though. Chrome's "Copy as cURL (bash)" uses `$'...'` exactly when a value contains a single quote, a newline or another special character, so these cases are common:

- `\n`, `\t`, `\r` and `\\` end up in the body as a literal backslash plus a letter.
- `\'` (Chrome's escaping for an apostrophe) leaves the quotes unbalanced after normalization, so `shlex` raises.

### Steps to Reproduce

```python
>>> from scrapy import Request
>>> Request.from_curl(r"curl https://x.io/p --data-raw $'line1\nline2'").body
b'line1\\nline2'
>>> Request.from_curl(r"""curl https://x.io/p --data-raw $'{"name":"O\'Brien"}'""")
ValueError: No closing quotation
```

### Expected behavior

The same bytes bash passes to curl: `b'line1\nline2'` and `b'{"name":"O\'Brien"}'`.

### Actual behavior

There's a literal `\n` in the body, and the second command raises `ValueError: No closing quotation`.

### Reproduces how often

Always.

### Versions

Scrapy 2.19.0, and main at 00ca2a9.

### Additional context

The [bash ANSI-C quoting rules](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/ANSI_002dC-Quoting.html) are short: `\a \b \e \E \f \n \r \t \v \\ \' \" \?`, `\nnn` (octal), `\xHH`, `\uHHHH`, `\UHHHHHHHH` and `\cX`. `_normalize_curl_command()` could decode the contents of `$'...'` and re-quote the result safely for `shlex`, instead of only dropping the `$`.

problem_statement:
In some cases reaching RESPONSE_MAX_ACTIVE_SIZE hangs the crawl
Since #6430, `DownloaderMiddlewareManager` subtracts the size of a response from the active size only in a [`weakref.finalize()` callback](https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/blob/2d22bf9ae9a2953bc55e017bc89f3ec469c820c8/scrapy/core/downloader/middleware.py#L142), that is, when the response is freed. A response that is part of a reference cycle is freed only by the cyclic garbage collector, which runs only as a side effect of allocations. Once [`needs_backout()`](https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/blob/2d22bf9ae9a2953bc55e017bc89f3ec469c820c8/scrapy/core/downloader/__init__.py#L287) pauses request processing, the process allocates next to nothing, so no collection runs and the crawl never resumes. The only output is one `Pausing request processing` INFO message. Running `gc.collect()` periodically makes the crawls below finish as fast as on 2.19.0.

Cases where this happens:

- **Error responses without an errback.** `HttpErrorMiddleware` raises `HttpError`, and [`call_spider_async()` re-raises the failure](https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/blob/2d22bf9ae9a2953bc55e017bc89f3ec469c820c8/scrapy/core/scraper.py#L387). The response is then held by the `HttpError`, which is held by the `Failure`, which is held by the `call_spider_async()` frame, which is held by the traceback of the exception. 100 × 300 KB 404 responses stall at about 50 pages; 300 × 100 KB don't stall.
- **Exceptions from middlewares.** A spider middleware raising in `process_spider_input()`, or a downloader middleware raising `IgnoreRequest` in `process_response()`, leaves the same kind of cycle.
- **Failed `FilesPipeline`/`ImagesPipeline` downloads.** These are non-200 responses, empty files, and images rejected by `IMAGES_MIN_*`. The media result cache keeps the `Failure` for the whole crawl, and [`cleanFailure()`](https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/blob/2d22bf9ae9a2953bc55e017bc89f3ec469c820c8/scrapy/pipelines/media.py#L251-L259) clears only the traceback of the outer exception, not the one of its `__context__` (`FileException`), whose frames hold the response. 150 items with a 100 KB 404 file each stall; with `MEDIA_CACHE_SIZE=0` they don't. With #8417, every later media request also waits for the 5-second bypass.
- **Cycles in spider code.** For example, `except ValueError as exc: error = exc` in a callback.
- **Responses kept by spider code.** For example, a response passed in `cb_kwargs` of scheduled requests. The setting docs warn about keeping responses, but they describe a soft limit, not a crawl that never resumes.

S3FilesStore can use a lot of memory
Hi,

@nramirezuy and me were debugging memory issue with one of the spiders  some time ago, and it seems to be caused by ImagesPipeline + [S3FilesStore](https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/blob/master/scrapy/contrib/pipeline/files.py#L66). I haven't confirmed that it was the cause of memory issue, this ticket is based solely on reading the source code.

FilesPipeline reads the whole file to memory and then defers the uploading to thread (via `S3FilesStore.persist_file`, passing file contents as bytes). So there could be many files loaded to memory at the same time, and as soon as files are downloaded faster than they are are uploaded to s3, memory usage will grow. This is not unlikely IMHO because s3 is not super-fast. For ImagesPipeline it is worse because it uploads not only the image itself, but also the generated thumbnails.

I think S3FilesStore should persist files to temporary location before uploading them to S3 (at least optionally). This would allow streaming files without storing them in memory.

Hey. It seems this CVE is popping up everywhere, and can cause some warnings for the users, so we should do something about it.

Let's investigate possible solutions. https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2017-14158 tells that the issue is an instance of https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/400.html. Description of CWE-400:

> The software does not properly control the allocation and maintenance of a limited resource, thereby enabling an actor to influence the amount of resources consumed, eventually leading to the exhaustion of available resources. 

> Limited resources include memory, file system storage, database connection pool entries, and CPU. If an attacker can trigger the allocation of these limited resources, **but the number or size of the resources is not controlled**, then the attacker could cause a denial of service that consumes all available resources. 

Scrapy controls the number and size of the resources in the following way:

1. There is DOWNLOAD_MAXSIZE (https://docs.scrapy.org/en/latest/topics/settings.html#download-maxsize) option, to prevent downloading large files.
2. There are various CONCURRENT_REQUESTS options, which allow to limit the amount of parallel downloads (each download then causes an upload to S3).
3. There is SCRAPER_SLOT_MAX_ACTIVE_SIZE, which is a soft limit for total size of all responses being processed by scraper ("While the sum of the sizes of all responses being processed is above this value, Scrapy does not process new requests."). I'm not sure though why is it applied on Scraper level, not on Downloader level. So, it seems this option doesn't have an effect if a request is added to downloader without going through scraper, and it seems requests initiated in MediaPipeline don't go through scraper.

Reducing the amount of RAM, e.g. storing more data to disk, is not a solution for CVE. By doing so we're shifting the resource from "memory usage" to "disk usage", without addressing the security issue. 

It seems that having an option similar to SCRAPER_SLOT_MAX_ACTIVE_SIZE, but which works on Downloader level or on Engine level should solve the problem. I.e. limit (in a soft way - if we're over limit, stop accepting new work) the total byte size of responses being processed by all Scrapy components. What do you think?
As for vulnerability, if the files/images pipelines or other components which add files to Downloader directly are not used, then it seems CWE-400 doesn't apply. There are DOWNLOAD_MAXSIZE and CONCURRENT_REQUESTS limits, and they look adequate according to the CWE-400 description.

I'm confused as to why this is even a security vulnerability. Are people habitually allowing third-parties (i.e. potential attackers) to cause crawls to start against arbitrary URLs? I just don't see how an attacker can DOS my system, considering it's (1) not publicly accessible, (2) all crawls are to constrained sets of URLs as configured in spiders, and (3) crawls are only initiated by a scheduler controlled by the admin (or scheduled by the admin directly). I would have assumed that most Scrapy usage fit these 3 assumptions. It feels a bit like a CVE about `tail`, because if a user gains access to a server they can run `tail /dev/zero` and exhaust memory...
The threat is sites that disapprove of being scraped and that could take deliberate measures to crash the scrapers, i.e. the threat actor is the site being scraped itself.
Hmm. Do general-use clients for internet protocols set memory limits? It seems like the same threat exists for anything that allows loading a large payload into memory, e.g. `requests`' `response.json()` method.
Assumption 2 is not entirely true for web scraping. URL discovery is often done as part of the crawling. A website detecting some activity as automated could indeed send special responses to a crawler, e.g. point a crawler to special URLs designed to mess with the crawling.

I don’t think this is a likely scenario, and I am not sure how much of a security issue this is, since websites doing something like this could expose themselves legally.

We still want to address the issue, though, because security aside, this can be an actual issue on normal websites.

problem_statement:
Scan the whole response for base URL and meta refresh on w3lib 2.5.0+
Resolves #3017.

We should also make a decision on what we want to do:
- Do we keep the current cap, change it or lift it?
- Do we use different caps for base URL and meta refresh?
- Do we allow users to override the cap? (if we do, for setting names we could use `HTML_MAX_SCAN` if 1 setting or `BASE_URL_MAX_SCAN` and `METAREFRESH_MAX_SCAN` if 2)

I had an LLM download the homepage of ~1k websites popular in terms of web scraping, plus listing pages and details pages for some of them, and gather data on what different caps would buy us, with w3lib 2.5.0, in terms of performance and coverage:

> I pulled data for this instead of guessing: 1512 pages from 906 of the top 1000 domains by usage, […], measuring where `<base href>` and the meta refresh tag actually sit in `response.text`.
>
> […]
>
> The two tags behave nothing alike, which I think settles it in favor of two separate settings:
>
> ```
> <base href>      present on   23/1512 pages (1.5%)     meta refresh   present on   64/1512 pages (4.2%)
>   p50    0.1 KB                                          p50    2.5 KB
>   p75    2.2 KB                                          p75   10.2 KB
>   p90    6.5 KB                                          p90  128.5 KB
>   p100 100.3 KB                                          p100 581.8 KB
>
> coverage by cap                                        coverage by cap
>    4 KB   82.6%     32 KB   91.3%                         4 KB   56.2%     32 KB   81.2%
>    8 KB   91.3%    128 KB  100.0%                         8 KB   75.0%    128 KB   89.1%
>   16 KB   91.3%    256 KB  100.0%                        16 KB   78.1%    256 KB   93.8%
> ```
>
> `<base href>` is rare and sits at the very top, so 8 KB gets 91% of it. A meta refresh can be anywhere, and our current 4096 misses 44% of them, i.e. about 1.8% of all pages have a meta refresh we silently ignore. That is a redirect the crawl never follows.
>
> Mean cost per response over the same corpus, from the measured linear scan rates:
>
> ```
>        cap    get_base_url    get_meta_refresh
>       4096       0.0013 ms         0.0034 ms
>       8192       0.0025 ms         0.0067 ms
>      32768       0.0100 ms         0.0266 ms
>     131072       0.0375 ms         0.0998 ms
>  unlimited       0.1612 ms         0.4294 ms
> ```
>
> I would default both to `0`, no limit, and leave the settings as the escape hatch for whoever cares about the 0.59 ms. Against a selector build on a 500 KB page that is single digit percent, and it is the only default that is right every time. [Mind that the LLM here has most likely been biased by my personal preference for correctness over performance]
>
> If we would rather cap by default, the knee points are 8192 for the base URL and 131072 for the meta refresh. Anything between 8 KB and 128 KB for the meta refresh pays for coverage it does not get, the curve is almost flat there.
>
> Two caveats. The `<base href>` numbers rest on 23 pages, so that tail is not really characterized, the p95 of 100 KB is one or two pages. And the corpus is 60% home pages, since my link heuristics only found a listing page for 44% of the domains and a detail page for 17%.

- [x] I have read the [contributing guide](https://docs.scrapy.org/en/master/contributing.html) and [set up pre-commit](https://docs.scrapy.org/en/master/contributing.html#pre-commit).

Entire HTML is not checked for finding base tag
In the HTML we are using the base tag is set. It also happens that this HTML has huge amount of comment and white space , and base tag is not coming in first 4096 characters.

In the code here - https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/blob/b8870ee8a10360aaa74298324d97c823b88ec5c6/scrapy/utils/response.py#L27

```
def get_base_url(response):
    """Return the base url of the given response, joined with the response url"""
    if response not in _baseurl_cache:
        text = response.text[0:4096]
        _baseurl_cache[response] = html.get_base_url(text, response.url,
            response.encoding)
    return _baseurl_cache[response]
```

We could find that , in the code above , we are NOT checking for the base tag beyond first 4096 characters. This has failed our crawl.
I believe there could not be any hard coding in any code and  I request to make this configurable atleast. 

We are stuck with this , please advice what needs to be done.

problem_statement:
robots.txt enforcement fails OPEN for 2nd+ concurrent same-host request (RobotsTxtMiddleware + Twisted Deferred.asFuture())
## What happened

With `ROBOTSTXT_OBEY=True`, a path disallowed by robots.txt was fetched (HTTP 200) instead of being blocked — but only when it was the **2nd or later concurrent request to the same host**. Reproduced 4/4 runs, deterministically.

**Versions:** Scrapy 2.19, Python 3.12 (Twisted as bundled with the Scrapy 2.19 install — exact version available on request).

## Reproduction

1. Serve a local test site (`python -m http.server`) with robots.txt containing:
```
User-agent: *
Disallow: /private/
```
2. Run a spider with `ROBOTSTXT_OBEY=True`, `DOWNLOAD_DELAY=1.0`, `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN=1`, AutoThrottle enabled, honest User-Agent, requesting three URLs on that host: a live page, a 404, and `/private/x.html`.
3. Observe: `/private/x.html` returns 200 and reaches the parse callback instead of being filtered by the robots middleware.

## Root cause (instrumented)

Concurrent same-host requests share a single Twisted `Deferred` for the robots.txt fetch/parse inside `RobotsTxtMiddleware`. The middleware converts that Deferred per-waiter via `Deferred.asFuture()` — and Twisted's `asFuture()` delivers the real result to the **first** future and **`None`** to the second. The second waiter therefore gets `parser=None`, and `process_request_2` treats `None` as "no parser available → allow the request."

So robots.txt enforcement **silently fails open** for every concurrent same-host request after the first, on the very first robots.txt fetch for a host.

## Expected behavior

All waiters on the shared robots.txt Deferred should receive the parsed result (or all should fail closed — block the request — if the parse result is unavailable).

## Suggested fix directions

- Share the *parsed* result (not the raw Deferred) across waiters; or
- Fail closed: treat `parser=None` as "deny" rather than "allow" in `process_request_2`.

## Workaround

Serialize same-host requests so two requests never race the first robots.txt fetch of a host (e.g. `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN=1` plus a per-host delay), or pre-fetch robots.txt before crawling.

## Why this matters

Fail-open robots.txt enforcement is a compliance footgun: users who set `ROBOTSTXT_OBEY=True` believe disallowed paths are never fetched. Under concurrency, that guarantee silently breaks.

---
*Found while building a polite liveness-checker that deliberately serializes per-host requests; the serialization accidentally immunized us, which is how the race was isolated. Happy to provide the minimal spider + test server scripts.*

Root cause: when concurrent same-host requests race the first robots.txt fetch, each waiter converts the shared `Deferred` to a future via `Deferred.asFuture()`. Twisted's `maybeSucceed` callback implicitly returns `None` after setting its own future, so the Deferred's chained result becomes `None` for the 2nd+ waiters — they see `parser is None` and `process_request_2` fails open. The fix re-reads `self._parsers[netloc]` (updated by `_parse_robots`/`_robots_error` before the Deferred fires) instead of trusting the awaited value. Includes a regression test with 3 concurrent requests.

problem_statement:
Deprecate or drop PyPy support
I never fully understood why we support it. The CI job for it is rather slow. We have had to do some minor hacks for PyPy, including their own dependencies, and [will have to make more](https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/pull/6430).

I feel like we should either deprecate it, to give users of PyPy + Scrapy a chance to convince us to keep it, or drop it altogether already.
hints_text:
AFAIK the only reason for PyPy support was its increased performance (ISTR some very old benchmarks in some of the Scrapy issues). I have no idea though, whether it still stands and whether anyone uses it.
Well I believe there are no furthur discussions. So i think this issue can be closed. @wRAR 
We don't have a ready-to-use way to compare performance of scrapy on pypy vs python-c implementations.

Scrapy suite (codspeed) can work with pypy only in wall-time mode, and brings issues: JIT warm-up, system noise, system-specific data. On my macOS, with 5s warm-up:
```bash
pytest tests/benchmarks/test_urls.py --codspeed --codspeed-warmup-time 5 --codspeed-max-time 10
```

Time spent during runtime (based on profiler):
- 35% in request fingerprinting for the dupefilter
- 20% link extraction (Lxml parse using C extension layer)

I think we want to disregard extraction comparison due to C extension usage. "Any C extension module recompiled with PyPy takes a very large hit in performance." https://pypy.org/performance.html (CPython C extension modules)
Pypy users probably use BeautifulSoup (with pure python backend) instead of lmxl.

I'm +1 for dropping PyPy from Scrapy, we can start with removing the CI jobs and the classifier, not sure if there is code we can remove that would break anything on PyPy (I assume removing the `PyPyDispatcher` dep will break it though). Not sure if there is anything to "deprecate" here, I don't want to add explicit checks and warnings.

For Scrapy deps, where official support and CI jobs were added specifically because they are Scrapy deps, we can keep or remove it, not sure if any of the deps are especiallu useful on PyPy but also they are unlikely to break just there.

The reason I'm writing this now is I tried to add a PyPy 3.12 job to several of our projects and it broke on building the lxml wheel (even for PyPy 3.11 in one case, because it's now 8.0.0, while the older published wheels are for 7.3). While it should be possible to fix on Linux by adding libxml-dev etc. I don't want to spend time working on this for multiple projects.

@kmike this is your last chance to block this :)
@lopuhin do you recall how did pypy speedups manifest? 
@kmike I couldn't find any results, AFAIK it was never covered by the 2017 GSoC project on scrapy benchmarking, and I personally also don't recall any measurements. Generally I wouldn't expect any crazy wins here, as normally most time would be spend outside of python.

problem_statement:
Handle get_event_loop() deprecation
Fixes #7201.
Get rid of get_event_loop()
`asyncio.get_event_loop()` is deprecated and in most cases we should use `get_running_loop()` instead, taking care not to run that code before the loop starts. 

Current uses:
* `AsyncCrawlerRunner._crawl()` - may need further refactoring, maybe together with `Crawler.crawl()`/`Crawler.crawl_async()`, but may require behavior changes in the latter
* `AsyncCrawlerProcess.start()`
* `AsyncioLoopingCall.start()`
* `call_later()`
* `deferred_to_future()`
* `_schedule_coro()`

problem_statement:
Request.from_curl() incorrectly strips a leading "$" from request data
<!--

Thanks for taking an interest in Scrapy!

If you have a question that starts with "How to...", please see the Scrapy Community page: https://scrapy.org/community/.
The GitHub issue tracker's purpose is to deal with bug reports and feature requests for the project itself.

Keep in mind that by filing an issue, you are expected to comply with Scrapy's Code of Conduct, including treating everyone with respect: https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/blob/master/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md

The following is a suggested template to structure your issue, you can find more guidelines at https://docs.scrapy.org/en/latest/contributing.html#reporting-bugs

-->

### Description

`Request.from_curl()` incorrectly removes a leading `$` character from
`-d`, `--data`, and `--data-raw` values when `$` is part of the actual
request data.

This silently changes the request body parsed from a valid cURL command.
This is especially problematic for OData-style request bodies, where names
such as `$top`, `$skip`, `$filter`, `$select`, and `$expand` are valid.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Run the following Python code:

```python
from scrapy import Request

request = Request.from_curl(
    "curl 'http://example.com/' --data-raw '$top=10&$skip=5'"
)

print(request.body)

problem_statement:
Refactor engine starting and stopping flow
Both the engine initialization and finalization are complicated multi-stage processes that also each have several separate top-level functions to call (`start()`/`start_async()` and `open_spider()`/`open_spider_async()`; `stop()`, `close()` and `close_spider()`). All of the involved code is also asynchronous. In most production runs that make a request this works fine and in a valid order, but in some cases, including early spider shutdown for various reasons (which are valid use cases) and early exceptions due to bugs (which is not an expected case but still should behave within certain expected standards) this breaks down with various outcomes, ranging from unexpected log messages to the spider process hanging. Over the years we identified and patched some of these, and wrote tests for some of them, but we don't test everything and even existing tests often depend on timing and aren't reliable.

A basic example of the problem is shutting down the spider via an early `self.crawler.engine.close_spider()` made in user code or in the `CloseSpider` extension before the starting up code is finished, leading to parts of `start()` running after some or all parts of `stop()` and `close_spider()`, which in turns may lead to e.g. hanging or (cascades of) unhandled AttributeErrors.
Ideally this flow should be made robust, so that at least the code never hangs, never swallows exceptions or bubbles up unhandled ones, and allows further modifications without an easy way to accidentally break it again. I feel like some state machine-based approach can help.

Some of the related issues are #1523 (there is important analysis there, that `engine_stopped` is always later than `spider_closed` but `engine_started` and `spider_opened` have different behavior in the shell than in normal spiders), #3435, #3343.

problem_statement:
Per-domain / per-slot concurrency is not enforced with the asyncio reactor when download delay is 0
## Description

With the asyncio reactor and no download delay, a download slot's concurrency limit is
not enforced.

In the reproduction below, `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN = 2` lets 18
requests to one host run at once; the server confirms it receives all 18 together. A
`DOWNLOAD_SLOTS` entry with `concurrency` and no `delay` behaves the same way, as it
goes through the same code.

Scrapy's own defaults hit this case (asyncio reactor, `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN = 8`,
`DOWNLOAD_DELAY = 0`). With them, the same script reaches up to 15 simultaneous requests
to one host against the limit of 8. The exact peak varies between runs, and
`CONCURRENT_REQUESTS = 16` caps how far it can go. Projects generated by `startproject` set
`DOWNLOAD_DELAY = 1`, which hides it.

## Steps to reproduce

Self-contained, no network access needed: it serves its own endpoint on localhost.

```python
"""Minimal reproduction: per-slot concurrency is not enforced when delay is 0.

Serves a local endpoint that holds each response open for HOLD seconds, sends
BURST requests to it with CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN = 2 and no download
delay, and reports the largest number of requests in flight at any one time,
both as Scrapy counts them (the slot) and as the server sees them.

    $ python mre.py                    # asyncio reactor -> peak 18, limit ignored
    $ DELAY=0.05 python mre.py         # non-zero delay  -> peak 2
    $ REACTOR=select python mre.py     # SelectReactor   -> peak 2
"""
import os
import threading
import time
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer

import scrapy
from scrapy.crawler import CrawlerProcess
from twisted.internet.task import LoopingCall

CONCURRENCY = 2
BURST = 20
HOLD = 0.25                                # how long each response is held open
DELAY = float(os.environ.get("DELAY", 0))  # DOWNLOAD_DELAY
REACTOR = {
    "asyncio": "twisted.internet.asyncioreactor.AsyncioSelectorReactor",
    "select": "twisted.internet.selectreactor.SelectReactor",
}[os.environ.get("REACTOR", "asyncio")]


_lock = threading.Lock()
_in_flight = 0
_server_peak = 0


class _Endpoint(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    protocol_version = "HTTP/1.1"

    def do_GET(self):
        global _in_flight, _server_peak
        with _lock:
            _in_flight += 1
            _server_peak = max(_server_peak, _in_flight)
        time.sleep(HOLD)
        with _lock:
            _in_flight -= 1
        body = b"ok"
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/plain")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)

    def log_message(self, *args):
        pass


_server = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), _Endpoint)
PORT = _server.server_address[1]
threading.Thread(target=_server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()


class BurstSpider(scrapy.Spider):
    name = "burst"
    custom_settings = {
        # Far above the per-domain limit, so the slot is the only thing that
        # could bound this traffic.
        "CONCURRENT_REQUESTS": 100,
        "CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN": CONCURRENCY,
        "DOWNLOAD_DELAY": DELAY,
        "LOG_LEVEL": "ERROR",
        "TWISTED_REACTOR": REACTOR,
    }

    peak = 0
    started = None

    async def start(self):
        self.started = time.monotonic()
        self._sampler = LoopingCall(self._sample)
        self._sampler.start(0.001)
        for i in range(BURST):
            yield scrapy.Request(f"http://127.0.0.1:{PORT}/{i}", dont_filter=True)

    def parse(self, response):
        return

    def _sample(self):
        slot = self.crawler.engine.downloader.slots.get("127.0.0.1")
        if slot is not None:
            self.peak = max(self.peak, len(slot.transferring))

    def closed(self, reason):
        self._sampler.stop()
        elapsed = time.monotonic() - self.started
        print(f"\n  reactor                     : {REACTOR.rsplit('.', 1)[-1]}")
        print(f"  download delay              : {DELAY}")
        print(f"  concurrency per domain      : {CONCURRENCY}")
        print(f"  requests sent               : {BURST}")
        print(f"  peak len(slot.transferring) : {self.peak}")
        print(f"  peak requests at the server : {_server_peak}")
        print(f"  elapsed                     : {elapsed:.2f}s "
              f"(at {CONCURRENCY} at a time: ~{BURST / CONCURRENCY * HOLD:.2f}s)\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    process = CrawlerProcess(settings={"TELNETCONSOLE_ENABLED": False})
    process.crawl(BurstSpider)
    process.start()
```

## Expected behaviour

No more than 2 requests in flight to the host at once, so 20 requests at 0.25 s each
take roughly 2.5 s.

## Actual behaviour

```
  reactor                     : AsyncioSelectorReactor
  download delay              : 0.0
  concurrency per domain      : 2
  requests sent               : 20
  peak len(slot.transferring) : 18          <- expected <= 2
  peak requests at the server : 18          <- expected <= 2
  elapsed                     : 0.54s       <- expected ~2.50s
```

Either a non-zero delay or a non-asyncio reactor gives the expected result, which is
what points at the cause:

```
$ DELAY=0.05 python mre.py
  peak len(slot.transferring) : 2
  peak requests at the server : 2
  elapsed                     : 2.63s

$ REACTOR=select python mre.py
  peak len(slot.transferring) : 2
  peak requests at the server : 2
  elapsed                     : 2.56s
```

The peak is 18 on almost every run, occasionally 19, depending on how many requests the
engine has fed before the first transfer registers.

## Diagnosis

`Downloader._process_queue`:

```python
while slot.queue and slot.free_transfer_slots() > 0:
    slot.lastseen = now
    request, queue_dfd = slot.queue.popleft()
    download_dfd = deferred_from_coro(
        self._wait_for_download(slot, request, queue_dfd)
    )
    ...
    # prevent burst if inter-request delays were configured
    if delay:
        self._process_queue(slot)
        break
```

`free_transfer_slots()` is `concurrency - len(slot.transferring)`, but
`slot.transferring.add(request)` happens inside `_download`. Under the asyncio reactor,
`deferred_from_coro` wraps the coroutine in an asyncio task, which doesn't start until
the loop yields. So `len(slot.transferring)` can't grow while this loop runs,
`free_transfer_slots()` returns the same value on every iteration, and the loop drains
the whole queue.

Two things hide it:

- **A delay.** The `if delay:` branch stops after one request and re-arms through
  `latercall`, so the count is up to date by the time the loop runs again.
- **A non-asyncio reactor.** There the coroutine runs straight away, up to its first
  real suspension, which is past the `transferring.add`, so the count is already current.

(In 2.18.0 the line is `_schedule_coro(...)`, which calls `loop.create_task` under
asyncio; same effect.)

## Possible fix

Counting a request as transferring when it is popped, rather than when its coroutine
starts, keeps `free_transfer_slots()` accurate inside the loop:

```diff
 request, queue_dfd = slot.queue.popleft()
+slot.transferring.add(request)
 download_dfd = deferred_from_coro(
```

`_download` already adds the request to the same set (a second add does nothing) and
removes it in its `finally`. 

When applying this in a fork, this gives:

| | slot peak | server peak | elapsed | responses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| master, `delay 0` | 18 | 18 | 0.53 s | 20/20 |
| patched, `delay 0` | **2** | **2** | 2.56 s | 20/20 |
| patched, `delay 0.05` | 2 | 2 | 2.64 s | 20/20 |
| patched, Scrapy defaults (limit 8) | 8 | 8 | 1.28 s | 40/40 |


## Versions

```
Scrapy       : 2.19.0
Python       : 3.12.14
Twisted      : 26.4.0
lxml         : 6.1.3
Platform     : macOS 27.0 (arm64)
Reactor      : twisted.internet.asyncioreactor.AsyncioSelectorReactor
```

problem_statement:
Response data is not released after processing?
Hello,

code sample:
```
def start_requests(self):
    for url in url_list:
            yield scrapy.Request(url=url, headers = xxx, callback=self.parse, errback=None,dont_filter=False)

def parse(self, response):
    ...
    response.xpath('//*[@id="feed-main-list"]/li')
    ...
```
If we call selector related function like xpath(...), the response data will not be released after parsing of each url.

In scrapy/http/response/text.py, 
```
class TextResponse(Response):
...
    def selector(self):
        from scrapy.selector import Selector
        if self._cached_selector is None:
            self._cached_selector = Selector(self)
        return self._cached_selector

    def xpath(self, query, **kwargs):
        return self.selector.xpath(query, **kwargs)
```
It has the cyclic reference like response -> Selector -> response.
In my rough test, if i don't use self._cached_selector to keep Selector object, the memory usage will reduce from 6x% -> 4x%. 

So, am i right? or how to understand it?

problem_statement:
Request priority not guaranteed with the default scheduler configurations due to different queues (memory/disk) used.
**Description**

Request priority not guaranteed with the default scheduler configurations due to different queues (memory/disk) used.

**Reproduction of the issue**

```
$ scrapy shell -s JOBDIR=/tmp/scrapytmp -s LOG_UNSERIALIZABLE_REQUESTS=0
(MULTIPLE LINES OMITTED HERE)
In [1]: schdlr = scrapy.core.scheduler.Scheduler.from_crawler(crawler)                                                                                                                        

In [2]: schdlr.open(spider)                                                                                                                                                                   

In [3]: schdlr.enqueue_request(scrapy.Request('http://a.com/mqs-0-unserializable', meta={'foo': lambda: 'bar'}, priority=0))                                                                  
Out[3]: True

In [4]: schdlr.enqueue_request(scrapy.Request('http://a.com/dqs-100', priority=100))                                                                                                          
Out[4]: True

In [5]: schdlr.next_request()                                                                                                                                                                 
Out[5]: <GET http://a.com/mqs-0-unserializable>

In [6]: schdlr.next_request()                                                                                                                                                                 
Out[6]: <GET http://a.com/dqs-100>
```

Scrapy version involved: c72ab1d (the current HEAD).

**Expected behavior**

The request with higher priority shall have come out first.

**Cause of the issue**

The scheduler maintains two queues (memory / disk) and the memory queue always have a higher priority when generating the next request.
Related code: https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/blob/c72ab1d/scrapy/core/scheduler.py#L66

Marking the Request: When ```RetryMiddleware``` creates a retry attempt, it adds a special, private flag (```_retry_dont_filter```) to that request's metadata. This acts as a signal that the ```dont_filter=True``` on this request is temporary and was set by the retry logic.

Checking the Signal: When ```RedirectMiddleware``` later processes a redirect for this exact request, it checks for the presence of that special flag.

Workaround for Issue #6895
This solution involves subclassing the default RetryMiddleware and RedirectMiddleware to create a "cooperative signal" that prevents the dont_filter flag from being incorrectly propagated after a retry.

Step 1: Create a middlewares.py file

In your Scrapy project's main directory (e.g., myproject/myproject/middlewares.py), add the following code:
Generated python

# myproject/middlewares.py
```python

from scrapy.downloadermiddlewares.redirect import RedirectMiddleware
from scrapy.downloadermiddlewares.retry import RetryMiddleware, get_retry_request

class ProjectRetryMiddleware(RetryMiddleware):
    """
    This middleware intelligently flags requests that it is retrying.
    It only adds the flag if it is the one setting dont_filter=True.
    """
    def _retry(self, request, reason, spider):
        # Check the state of dont_filter on the *original* failing request.
        dont_filter_was_set = request.dont_filter

        new_request = get_retry_request(
            request,
            reason=reason,
            spider=spider,
            max_retry_times=self.max_retry_times,
            priority_adjust=self.priority_adjust,
        )

        # Only add the meta flag if we are the ones changing the dont_filter state.
        if new_request and not dont_filter_was_set:
            new_request.meta['_retry_dont_filter'] = True

        return new_request

class ProjectRedirectMiddleware(RedirectMiddleware):
    """
    This middleware respects the flag set by ProjectRetryMiddleware.
    It prevents the propagation of a temporary dont_filter flag to a redirected request.
    """
    def _redirect(self, redirected, request, spider, reason):
        # Check if the dont_filter flag was temporarily set by our retry middleware.
        is_temporary_retry = request.meta.get('_retry_dont_filter', False)
        
        # If it was a temporary retry, do not propagate dont_filter.
        # Otherwise, respect the original request's dont_filter value.
        redirected.dont_filter = request.dont_filter and not is_temporary_retry
        
        # Call the rest of the original _redirect method, but without the dont_filter logic.
        # We can't call super()._redirect() as it would re-apply the flawed logic.
        ttl = request.meta.setdefault("redirect_ttl", self.max_redirect_times)
        redirects = request.meta.get("redirect_times", 0) + 1

        if ttl and redirects <= self.max_redirect_times:
            redirected.meta["redirect_times"] = redirects
            redirected.meta["redirect_ttl"] = ttl - 1
            redirected.meta["redirect_urls"] = [
                *request.meta.get("redirect_urls", []),
                request.url,
            ]
            redirected.meta["redirect_reasons"] = [
                *request.meta.get("redirect_reasons", []),
                reason,
            ]
            redirected.priority = request.priority + self.priority_adjust
            self.logger.debug(
                "Redirecting (%(reason)s) to %(redirected)s from %(request)s",
                {"reason": reason, "redirected": redirected, "request": request},
                extra={"spider": spider},
            )
            return redirected
        
        self.logger.debug(
            "Discarding %(request)s: max redirections reached",
            {"request": request},
            extra={"spider": spider},
        )
        raise IgnoreRequest("max redirections reached")
```

+def _fake_ftp(
+    retr_reply: bytes, data: bytes = b""
+) -> Callable[[asyncio.StreamReader, asyncio.StreamWriter], Any]:
+    """Return a minimal FTP server connection handler that sends *data*, if
+    any, and then answers RETR with *retr_reply*."""
+
+    async def handle(
+        reader: asyncio.StreamReader, writer: asyncio.StreamWriter
+    ) -> None:
+        data_writer: asyncio.Future[asyncio.StreamWriter] = (
+            asyncio.get_running_loop().create_future()
+        )
+
+        def on_data_connection(
+            _: asyncio.StreamReader, w: asyncio.StreamWriter
+        ) -> None:
+            data_writer.set_result(w)
+
+        writer.write(b"220 Ready\r\n")
+        while line := await reader.readline():
+            command = line.split()[0].upper()
+            if command == b"USER":
+                writer.write(b"230 Logged in\r\n")
+            elif command == b"TYPE":
+                writer.write(b"200 OK\r\n")
+            elif command == b"EPSV":
+                data_server = await asyncio.start_server(
+                    on_data_connection, "127.0.0.1", 0
+                )
+                port = data_server.sockets[0].getsockname()[1]
+                writer.write(f"229 Entering passive mode (|||{port}|)\r\n".encode())
+            elif command == b"RETR":
+                w = await data_writer
+                if data:
+                    writer.write(b"150 Sending\r\n")
+                    w.write(data)
+                w.close()
+                data_server.close()
+                writer.write(retr_reply)
+            await writer.drain()
+        writer.close()
+
+    return handle

Sitemap spider support for URLs beginning with double slash
Sitemap spider fails with urls starting with double slash:

raise ValueError('Missing scheme in request url: %s' % self._url)

hints_text:
Probably won't be handled, see my belonging pull request.

The sitemap owner is wrong, because from sitemaps.org, the <loc> field _must_ begin with a scheme: "This URL must begin with the protocol (such as http) and end with a trailing slash, if your web server requires it"

If there are such sitemaps in real world I think it makes sense to support them even if they violate some standard.

Ok, then I'll try it with a middleware. Hope this is the way to go.

@aufziehvogel I would modify `process_links` to receive response as an argument. So if you need to join relative urls you can do it there when its needed. As implementation goes it isn't backwards compatible at least you do some hacking; how i would manage that is by checking at one point if the function expect the argument using [`get_func_args`](https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/blob/master/scrapy/utils/python.py#L134) if the function doesn't expect response print a warning. So after couple of versions we can remove that check without breaking people spiders.

@nramirezuy Is it then okay to move `Rule` to a higher level and also use it in `SitemapSpider`? because currently `Rule` is defined in `crawl.py` only for the `CrawlSpider`. And I think you mean the `process_links` of `Rule`?

And am I getting you right, that you prefer a solution where the link correction itself is not part of scrapy core, but we only adjust the API so users can implement the correction themselves if they want to?

@aufziehvogel Sorry I got confused with `Rule`, `LinkExtractor` and `SitemapSpider` not using either. Promoting `Rule`might be too much work, if you want to do it go ahead. A much simpler to implement approach would be adding another attribute to define link manipulation. 

Example:

``` python
class FooSpider(SitemapSpider):
    sitemap_process_links = [('<regex>', function)]
```

problem_statement:
Provide a way to propagate an exit code from a Spider
I think we need a way to propagate the exit code from the Spider.

Based on: #1231
hints_text:
I like this idea. 

We can't do it from Spider because spider doesn't necessarily terminate the process - it is CrawlerProcess who does that.So we may need to expose CrawlerProcess to the spider. See also: https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/issues/1226

Well what I mean was terminate the process and be able to add an exit code with the outcome. We already have an [exception](https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/blob/master/scrapy/exceptions.py#L23) to terminate the process from the spider.

This exception stops the spider, not necessarily terminates the process. You can have multiple spiders in the same process running at the same time.

In our case, an exception is being thrown by an external API call in the `start_requests` method. The spider is being invoked using a `subprocess.check_call` that uses the `scrapy crawl spname` command. The exception is not bubbling up to the crawler process that invokes it, resulting in a 0 exit code. Do you guys have any thoughts about how this issue? Can you point me to where I can look?

I am interested in submitted a pull request and am looking for your guidance in implementing it.

problem_statement:
Image pipeline should allow to decide whether to auto-convert to jpg or not
Not 100% it's accurate, but the issue got reported here:

https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=10941213

> Image pipeline converts to jpg automatically. Cannot be disabled without writing all the image code yourself
hints_text:
I guess we refer to this [line](https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/blob/master/scrapy/pipelines/images.py#L106)

@dangra I set this to discuss because I'm not sure if there is any valid reason to force 'JPEG'.

something along thoses lines was proposed in https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/pull/250
but there was no followup since

One way to disable auto-convert to .jpg is to use FilesPipeline. The only drawback is that another features from ImagesPipeline can't be used with this approach. 

It makes sense that someone may want to use the features provided by ImagesPipeline but not auto-convert. I think a good solution that maintains backward compatibility is to provide a `IMAGES_CONVERT_TO` option that defaults to `JPG` and accepts `NONE`. And it could also allows to convert to another formats...

problem_statement:
Fix timezone handling in `FilesPipeline` stores
Found in https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/pull/8182#discussion_r4053447020

Various `FilesPipeline` stores produce the `last_modifed` value as the UNIX timestamp and some or all of them may do it incorrectly, depending on what are the values returned by S3 and GCS and what is in FTP `MDTM`. Their tests may also hide these problems and may need to be improved.

problem_statement:
Add possibility to use Selector (bytes) added in parsel 1.8.0.
## Summary

Please review possibility to apply RAM memory efficient Selector that can accept `bytes` as input 
added as result of https://github.com/scrapy/parsel/issues/210 (added in parsel 1.8.0) in scrapy (as default)

Currently UnifiedSelector (subclass of parsel's Selector used in scrapy) configured to use Response.text as input
Response.text (property) -> creates new object (Response.body -> converted to str) which is memory intensive and not needed 
https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/blob/5a37af146f4f036168ac562918fca43adb4ac65f/scrapy/selector/unified.py#L66-L73

## Motivation

As mentioned on https://github.com/scrapy/parsel/issues/210 usage of `str` input for creating Selector object is more RAM memory intensive

## Describe alternatives you've considered

At this stage it will require to.. separately create Selector object with bytes input inside spiders callback method (and not use Response.Selector)

## Additional context
Removing other usages of Response.text will significantly reduce RAM required to processing response

We've discussed this briefly yesterday and found that this may not be useful if we detect the response encoding at the same time as converting body to str (I think the relevant code is at https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/blob/5a37af146f4f036168ac562918fca43adb4ac65f/scrapy/http/response/text.py#L105 ?). We didn't do any extensive analysis of this though.
As we can see from

https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/blob/5a37af146f4f036168ac562918fca43adb4ac65f/scrapy/http/response/text.py#L62-L72

Response object with valid encoding received without call of `_body_inferred_encoding` (with conversion to unicode `str` ) has `_cached_ubody` as `None` and `encoding` (`not None`).

It means that on unified Selector `__init__` we can safely create `bytes` based selector for Response objects that match values mentioned above (and parsel v.1.8.0) and probably maintain current behaviour for other (w. encoding received from `_body_inferred_encoding` call) Response objects

https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/blob/5a37af146f4f036168ac562918fca43adb4ac65f/scrapy/selector/unified.py#L66-L83

hello @pczhaoyun , sorry for this very very very late feedback.
If you're still having this problem, can you explain a bit more what you're experiencing and what is not correct in your view with how media is downloaded? Sorry I don't understand it from your description and comment.

Not sure if this is 100% what @pczhaoyun meant, but looks like ``MediaPipeline`` caches results of ``media_downloaded`` method permanently into ``info.downloaded``: https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/blob/1.4.0/scrapy/pipelines/media.py#L143 and I don't see if this is removed anywhere (definitely not in this module, and search does not turn up any other places where it might be removed).
I observe this caching in practice too, with a slightly extended pipeline (https://github.com/TeamHG-Memex/scrapy-cdr/blob/d2150e5ae09b555da0eb53bf5dcbb248181b7c0d/scrapy_cdr/media_pipeline.py#L15). I think this applies to default pipeline as well, did not check yet.
Indeed, looks like there's unconditional caching. Makes sense to be able to disable it.
I would also disable it by default but that's backwards incompatible...
We could also give the user an option to limit the maximal number of cached items - that's what I would prefer in my use case (although it's easy to override if needed). I'm fine with some constant memory overhead in oder to avoid downloading same media items again, but would not like it to grow.
I had been facing the same issue, so far the simplest solution I found is inside `item_completed`, after getting all things done, reset downloaded to empty. `self.spiderinfo.downloaded = {}`, memory leak issue resolved.

problem_statement:
Improving headers values decoding (utf-8 vs latin1)
This raises from https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/issues/2589 where a server returns a non-UTF-8 header value. According to [this RFC](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-3.2.4):

>    Historically, HTTP has allowed field content with text in the
   ISO-8859-1 charset [ISO-8859-1], supporting other charsets only
   through use of [RFC2047] encoding.  In practice, most HTTP header
   field values use only a subset of the US-ASCII charset [USASCII].
   Newly defined header fields SHOULD limit their field values to
   US-ASCII octets.  A recipient SHOULD treat other octets in field
   content (obs-text) as opaque data.

So the `latin1` encoding may be preferred over `utf-8` which is the Scrapy's default.  At the other hand, `requests` in some places uses `utf-8` with a fallback to `latin1`: https://github.com/kennethreitz/requests/blob/d6f4818c0b40bc6c00433c013b7daaea83b2cd51/requests/models.py#L908

Following @kmike's [suggestion](https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/pull/2588#issuecomment-282112022), it seems that decoding headers with `utf-8` having `iso-8859-1` as fallback is the best option.
hints_text:
See PR https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/pull/2593 as a proposed implementation. The nice thing about this one is that, when dealing with non-UTF8 strings, it doesn't require user intervention as with #2588.

problem_statement:
move more functions from scrapy.utils.url to w3lib
Hey,

What do you think about moving `add_http_if_no_scheme` and `escape_ajax` functions to w3lib?
hints_text:
Good idea for `escape_ajax`, looks generic and useful enough. (Should we also have an `unescape_ajax`?)
I'm not sure about `add_http_if_no_scheme()`. Would it be useful outside of scrapy? Also one couldargue why it adds "http://" and not "https://".

I'm using `add_http_if_no_scheme` in pretty much every project where user provides a URL as an input. I think it should add http, not https because this is what browsers add if you enter a URL without a schema to the address bar. Many websites don't work with https, so adding https to a user-provided URL is likely to break it; sites which work with https often provide a redirect from http to https version anyways.

hm, what's the use case for unescape_ajax?

> hm, what's the use case for unescape_ajax?

I was thinking to make ajax-escaped URLs more readable. Is `_escaped_fragment_` still that commonly used anyway?

Also, we have a couple of dual functions in `w3lib.url` already (`add_or_replace_parameter`/`url_query_parameter`, `file_uri_to_path`/`path_to_file_uri`)

I think Google deprecated `_escaped_fragment_`, but as there are sites who support it escape_ajax can still be useful for crawling.

unescape_ajax looks less useful because there are no ajax-escaped links on websites. It may be helpful to parse logs though. But I'd not implement it unless we have a real use case.

problem_statement:
Let downloader middlewares process exceptions from process_response()
I am not sure if we really need it, and if so, what the best approach is.

I thought about a new process_response_exception() method that works in the same direction as process_exception() (lower priority middlewares get called), but I am not 100% sure, and I imagine we would still need to let the download handler exceptions go to process_exception() as I think they do now.

If that’s the way to go, I wonder if there is a deprecation path that we could go towards letting download handlers get their exception handled by the right middleware (semantically) going forward.

On the other hand, maybe the way to go is to have process_exception() get those exceptions as well, it would keep things simpler. But for backward-compatibility, maybe we should have a period where the new behavior is opt-in until we make it THE behavior.

Issues this may solve or help solving:
- https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/issues/1900
- https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/issues/2578 (could be solved separately, although it probably makes sense to tackle it while at it, since the code involved is the same)
- https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/issues/3506
- https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/issues/5078
- https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/issues/6990 (not sure if it needs solving, though)

RetryMiddleware doesn't actually retry HttpCompressionMiddleware errors

```

when including IOError in the exceptions to retry.

But IOError would be raised in HttpCompressionMiddleware's `process_response()`, errors from which are not handled by `process_exception()` in downloader middlewares.

```
self.crawler.stop()
return None

which requires to make `self.crawler` available in the `DownloaderMiddleware` via:
```
    def __init__(self, crawler):

My code to handle closespider in mw, according to this nice post:
```python
class ExampleMiddleware:

    def __init__(self, crawler):
        self.crawler = crawler

    @classmethod
    def from_crawler(cls, crawler):
        return cls(crawler)

    def process_response(self, request, response, spider):
        if response.status == 444:
            # bad response found
            self.crawler.engine.close_spider(spider, response.text)
            raise IgnoreRequest
``` 
> When a certain closing condition is met, requests which are currently in the downloader queue (up to [CONCURRENT_REQUESTS](https://docs.scrapy.org/en/2.11/topics/settings.html#std-setting-CONCURRENT_REQUESTS) requests) **are still processed**.

This behaviour documented on [docs](https://docs.scrapy.org/en/2.11/topics/extensions.html#module-scrapy.extensions.closespider) as expected.
Changed by https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/pull/4836  https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/issues/2759
an extension to inVains code, you can make your own `close_spider()` method in the Downloader Middleware and have it be executed after the spider closes. 

```
# middleware.py

@classmethod
def from_crawler(cls, crawler):
     ...
     # some code
     ...

     mw = cls(arg1, arg2, arg3)
     crawler.signals.connect(mw.close_spider, signal=signals.spider_closed)
     return mw

def close_spider(self, spider):
     spider.logger.info("Spider is closing from Downloader Middleware")
```

Here is the documentation - https://docs.scrapy.org/en/latest/topics/signals.html
